--- title: "Tutorial 6 · Evaluation, calibration and explanation" subtitle: "Session 7 · Day 2, 11.50–13.00 · Slides 07" --- ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## What you will do Evaluate the tuned XGBoost the way a clinician needs it evaluated: the confusion matrix at *this* prevalence, ROC against precision–recall, Brier score and **calibration**, a decision threshold chosen for a screening programme, the honest version of "class imbalance"; then explain the model globally (importance, partial dependence) and locally (SHAP) — with code that works unchanged for the neural network this afternoon. **Time:** 30 min live coding + 10 min *Your turn*. ::: ## 0 · Start ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # WHERE WE ARE --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Pipeline (T1), three families (T2-T4), tuning (T5). From here on the model is fixed: the tuned XGBoost from T5 # (loaded below from outputs/, with a fallback so this page also stands alone). NEW TODAY: judging it the way a # clinician needs - confusion matrix at the real prevalence, ROC vs PR, calibration, choosing a threshold on # purpose, class imbalance - and explaining it (importance, partial dependence, SHAP). source("R/prep_nhms.R") library(probably) # calibration, thresholds library(themis) # class-imbalance recipe steps library(DALEXtra) # model-agnostic explanations for tidymodels library(shapviz) # SHAP plots library(patchwork) library(future) plan(multisession, workers = max(1, parallel::detectCores() - 1)) dir.create("outputs", showWarnings = FALSE) # the tuned XGBoost from Tutorial 5 (falls back to a fixed sensible version so this page stands alone) if (file.exists("outputs/t05_xgb_last.rds")) { xgb_last <- readRDS("outputs/t05_xgb_last.rds") } else { xgb_spec <- boost_tree(trees = 500, learn_rate = 0.03, tree_depth = 3, min_n = 20, sample_size = 0.8) |> set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("classification") set.seed(2026) xgb_last <- last_fit(workflow(dm_rec, xgb_spec), dm_split, metrics = cls_metrics) } xgb_fit <- extract_workflow(xgb_last) # fitted workflow (recipe + model) xgb_final_wf <- workflow(dm_rec, extract_spec_parsnip(xgb_fit)) # same spec, unfitted, for resampling test_preds <- collect_predictions(xgb_last) # predictions on the locked test set # out-of-fold predictions on the TRAINING set: every DECISION (threshold, calibration) is made on these, # so the test set stays an honest final exam set.seed(2026) xgb_cv <- fit_resamples(xgb_final_wf, dm_folds, metrics = cls_metrics, control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) cv_preds <- collect_predictions(xgb_cv) ``` ::: ## 1 · A model is a probability; a decision is a threshold ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} test_preds |> select(undx_dm, .pred_Yes, .pred_class) |> head() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Every classifier we built outputs **P(Yes)**; `.pred_class` is just `P(Yes) ≥ 0.5`. The 0.5 is a software default that silently assumes a false positive and a false negative cost the same. In screening they never do. So we evaluate the probabilities (discrimination, calibration) *and* the decision (confusion matrix at the threshold we will actually use) — separately. ## 2 · The confusion matrix at the default threshold — and why it misleads ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} test_preds |> conf_mat(undx_dm, .pred_class) |> autoplot(type = "heatmap") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_evaluation_files/figure-html/confmat-1.png){width=960} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} test_preds |> conf_mat(undx_dm, .pred_class) |> summary() |> filter(.metric %in% c("accuracy", "sens", "spec", "ppv", "npv", "j_index")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Accuracy near 0.89 looks fine and is worthless: 88 % of people are *No*. Sensitivity at 0.5 is poor. Nobody told the model that missing a diabetic costs more than an extra blood test. | Metric | Also called | Asks | |---|---|---| | sensitivity | recall, TPR | of the people who have it, how many did we flag? | | specificity | TNR | of the people who don't, how many did we leave alone? | | PPV | precision | of the people we flagged, how many have it? | | NPV | — | of the people we cleared, how many are truly clear? | | J (Youden) | — | sens + spec − 1 | ### PPV is not a property of the model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ppv_at <- function(sens, spec, prev) (sens * prev) / (sens * prev + (1 - spec) * (1 - prev)) tibble(prevalence = c(0.02, 0.05, 0.116, 0.25)) |> mutate(ppv = ppv_at(sens = 0.80, spec = 0.75, prev = prevalence)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Same sensitivity and specificity, four populations, four PPVs. A model validated in a clinic (25 %) and deployed at a pasar malam (4 %) will see its PPV collapse. **Report the prevalence you validated at** — TRIPOD+AI asks for exactly this. ## 3 · Threshold-free: ROC, precision–recall, gain ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} roc_auc(test_preds, undx_dm, .pred_Yes); pr_auc(test_preds, undx_dm, .pred_Yes) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} p_roc <- roc_curve(test_preds, undx_dm, .pred_Yes) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "ROC") p_pr <- pr_curve(test_preds, undx_dm, .pred_Yes) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Precision-recall (baseline = 0.116)") p_gain <- gain_curve(test_preds, undx_dm, .pred_Yes) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Gain: screen the top x%, find y% of cases") p_roc + p_pr + p_gain ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_evaluation_files/figure-html/curves-1.png){width=1440} ::: ::: - **ROC** is prevalence-blind — good for comparing models across populations, flattering on rare outcomes. - **Precision–recall** shows what the positive predictions are *worth*; its baseline is the prevalence. - **Gain** is the one for a programme manager: "if we can only test 20 % of adults, which 20 %, and what share of cases do we catch?" ## 4 · Calibration: do the probabilities mean what they say? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} brier_class(test_preds, undx_dm, .pred_Yes) # 0 = perfect; predicting the prevalence for everyone gives ~0.10 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cal_plot_breaks(test_preds, truth = undx_dm, estimate = .pred_Yes, num_breaks = 10) + labs(title = "Reliability diagram, test set") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_evaluation_files/figure-html/calibration-1.png){width=960} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cal_plot_windowed(test_preds, truth = undx_dm, estimate = .pred_Yes) + labs(title = "Windowed calibration, test set") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_evaluation_files/figure-html/calibration-2.png){width=960} ::: ::: A point at (0.40, 0.25) means: when the model says 40 %, only 25 % actually have it. A model can have AUC 0.86 and still be badly calibrated — boosted trees and forests routinely are, and SMOTE'd models always are. A probability a clinician will *show* to a patient must be calibrated; a score that only sorts a queue cares less. ### Fix it honestly: estimate on CV predictions, validate within resamples ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cal_val <- cal_validate_logistic(xgb_cv, smooth = FALSE, metrics = metric_set(brier_class, roc_auc), save_pred = TRUE) # smooth = FALSE -> Platt (2 parameters) collect_metrics(cal_val) # uncalibrated vs calibrated: Brier down, AUC unchanged ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} collect_predictions(cal_val) |> cal_plot_breaks(truth = undx_dm, estimate = .pred_Yes, .by = .type) + labs(title = "Before vs after logistic recalibration (CV)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_evaluation_files/figure-html/recalibrate-1.png){width=960} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} calibrator <- cal_estimate_logistic(cv_preds, truth = undx_dm, smooth = FALSE) # fitted on out-of-fold predictions test_preds_cal <- cal_apply(test_preds, calibrator) # applied to the test set bind_rows(raw = brier_class(test_preds, undx_dm, .pred_Yes), calibrated = brier_class(test_preds_cal, undx_dm, .pred_Yes), .id = "probs") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Recalibration moves the probabilities, not the ranking: AUC is untouched, Brier improves, thresholds become meaningful. Platt/logistic (`smooth = FALSE`: two parameters, robust) for most cases; `probably`'s default (`smooth = TRUE`) fits a spline-based GAM and is more flexible; isotonic when you have lots of data and a strange shape. ## 5 · Choosing a threshold on purpose ![](../images/gen/threshold_tradeoff.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} thr_cv <- threshold_perf(cv_preds, undx_dm, .pred_Yes, thresholds = seq(0.02, 0.60, by = 0.01)) thr_cv |> filter(.metric %in% c("sensitivity", "specificity", "j_index")) |> ggplot(aes(.threshold, .estimate, colour = .metric)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = 2) + labs(title = "Sensitivity / specificity by threshold (CV predictions)", x = "threshold on P(Yes)", y = NULL) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_evaluation_files/figure-html/threshold-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: A community screen wants sensitivity around 0.80 and accepts the extra blood tests. Find the threshold on the **CV** predictions, then report it on the test set: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} thr_chosen <- thr_cv |> filter(.metric == "sensitivity", .estimate >= 0.80) |> slice_max(.threshold, n = 1) |> pull(.threshold) thr_chosen ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} test_thr <- test_preds |> mutate(.pred_screen = make_two_class_pred(.pred_Yes, levels = levels(undx_dm), threshold = thr_chosen) |> as.factor()) test_thr |> conf_mat(undx_dm, .pred_screen) |> summary() |> filter(.metric %in% c("sens", "spec", "ppv", "npv")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} test_thr |> summarise(flagged_pct = mean(.pred_screen == "Yes"), cases_found = sum(.pred_screen == "Yes" & undx_dm == "Yes") / sum(undx_dm == "Yes"), number_needed_to_screen = 1 / mean(undx_dm[.pred_screen == "Yes"] == "Yes")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: "Test the X % the model flags and you find Y % of the undiagnosed cases; about Z people tested per case found." That is a sentence a programme manager can act on. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Decision curve analysis (the clinician's metric) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} if (requireNamespace("dcurves", quietly = TRUE)) { dcurves::dca(undx_dm ~ .pred_Yes, data = test_preds |> mutate(undx_dm = undx_dm == "Yes"), thresholds = seq(0.02, 0.5, by = 0.01), label = list(.pred_Yes = "XGBoost")) |> plot(smooth = TRUE) } ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_evaluation_files/figure-html/dca-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: Net benefit at threshold *t* = (TP − FP × t/(1−t)) / n: the threshold *is* the exchange rate between a false and a true positive. A model is useful only where its curve sits above both "test everyone" and "test no one". ::: ## 6 · Class imbalance: the honest version ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lr_spec <- logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm") rec_smote <- dm_rec |> step_smote(undx_dm, over_ratio = 1) # only applied to training data (skip = TRUE) rec_down <- dm_rec |> step_downsample(undx_dm, under_ratio = 1) set.seed(2026) imbalance_res <- workflow_set(preproc = list(base = dm_rec, smote = rec_smote, downsample = rec_down), models = list(logistic = lr_spec)) |> workflow_map("fit_resamples", resamples = dm_folds, metrics = cls_metrics, seed = 2026) collect_metrics(imbalance_res) |> filter(.metric %in% c("roc_auc", "brier_class", "sensitivity", "specificity")) |> select(wflow_id, .metric, mean) |> pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = mean) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ![](../images/gen/smote_shifts_probabilities.png){fig-align="center" width="65%"} Balancing the training set pushes sensitivity-at-0.5 up — and AUC does not move while the Brier score gets **worse**, because every probability now thinks prevalence is 50 %. You got the same sensitivity in §5 by moving the threshold, without breaking calibration. SMOTE is a last resort; if you use it, recalibrate afterwards. ## 7 · Explaining the model: global ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} xgboost::xgb.importance(model = extract_fit_engine(xgb_fit)) |> # Gain = share of the total loss reduction attributed to each column as_tibble() |> slice_max(Gain, n = 15) |> ggplot(aes(Gain, reorder(Feature, Gain))) + geom_col(fill = "#0b4f6c") + labs(x = "gain (share of total loss reduction)", y = NULL, title = "XGBoost gain importance (model-specific)") + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_evaluation_files/figure-html/xgb-importance-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: Model-**agnostic** tools work for anything with a `predict()` — including this afternoon's network: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} explainer <- explain_tidymodels( xgb_fit, data = dm_train |> select(-undx_dm), y = dm_train$undx_dm == "Yes", predict_function_target_column = "Yes", # our event level; DALEX would otherwise take the 2nd column label = "XGBoost (tuned)", verbose = FALSE ) set.seed(2026) vi_perm <- model_parts(explainer, loss_function = DALEX::loss_one_minus_auc, B = 10, N = 1000) plot(vi_perm, max_vars = 15) + labs(title = "Permutation importance: AUC lost when a column is shuffled") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_evaluation_files/figure-html/dalex-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: Correlated predictors share credit (BMI, waist, weight, `bmi_cat` each look weaker than "adiposity" is). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pdp <- model_profile(explainer, variables = c("age", "bmi", "waist"), N = 500) plot(pdp) + labs(title = "Partial dependence: average predicted P(Yes) as one variable moves") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_evaluation_files/figure-html/pdp-1.png){width=960} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} pdp_sex <- model_profile(explainer, variables = "waist", groups = "sex", N = 500) plot(pdp_sex) + labs(title = "Waist by sex: two different cut-offs") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_evaluation_files/figure-html/pdp-2.png){width=960} ::: ::: Look for the structure the trees found: the BMI step near 27.5, the age plateau, two waist curves for two sexes. The last one is an interaction a logistic model never saw unless someone hand-coded sex-specific cut-offs. ## 8 · Explaining the model: local (SHAP) ::: {.callout-note} A **Shapley value** (game theory, 1953) is a variable's fair share of the difference between *this* person's prediction and the average prediction, averaged over every order in which the variables could be "added". The shares add up exactly to the prediction. Two ways to get them: **TreeSHAP** reads them *exactly* off a tree ensemble in well under a second (what we do here); **KernelSHAP** *estimates* them for any model from predictions alone (Tutorial 7 uses it on the neural network — same plots, slower estimator). One mechanical point first. The model never saw `sex` or `ethnic`; it saw the **baked** matrix the recipe produced — imputed, dummy-coded, normalised. SHAP values therefore come out per dummy column (`sex_Male`, `ethnic_Chinese`, …). `shapviz` can add the pieces of each factor back together (`collapse`) so you read one value per *original* variable, and plot it against the original, un-normalised values (`X`). ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # 1. the people to explain, and the matrix the model actually saw for them set.seed(2026) X_explain <- dm_train |> select(-undx_dm) |> slice_sample(n = 500) # 500 people is plenty for the plots rec_fit <- extract_recipe(xgb_fit) # the recipe as TRAINED inside the workflow X_baked <- bake(rec_fit, new_data = X_explain, all_predictors(), composition = "matrix") # 2. which dummy columns came from which factor (recipes keeps the book) -> one SHAP value per original variable dummy_step <- tidy(rec_fit) |> filter(type == "dummy") |> pull(number) facs <- tidy(rec_fit, number = dummy_step) |> pull(terms) |> unique() # the original factor columns # each factor -> the dummy columns it produced. bake() cleans the level names (25-29.9 -> X25.29.9), so match on # the "_" prefix of the ACTUAL baked columns rather than on the raw level names. collapse <- setNames(lapply(facs, \(f) grep(paste0("^", f, "_"), colnames(X_baked), value = TRUE)), facs) collapse <- collapse[lengths(collapse) > 0] # 3. TreeSHAP: exact Shapley values straight from the fitted trees sv <- shapviz(extract_fit_engine(xgb_fit), X_pred = X_baked, X = X_explain, collapse = collapse) sv_importance(sv, kind = "beeswarm", max_display = 15) + labs(title = "SHAP summary: each dot is one person") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_evaluation_files/figure-html/shap-1.png){width=960} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sv_dependence(sv, v = "bmi", color_var = "fam_hx_dm") + labs(title = "BMI, coloured by family history") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_evaluation_files/figure-html/shap-2.png){width=960} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sv_dependence(sv, v = "waist", color_var = "sex") + labs(title = "Waist, coloured by sex") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_evaluation_files/figure-html/shap-3.png){width=960} ::: ::: One patient: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} X_explain[1, c("age", "sex", "bmi", "waist", "fam_hx_dm", "ethnic")] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sv_waterfall(sv, row_id = 1) + labs(title = "Why this person scored what they scored") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_evaluation_files/figure-html/shap-local-1.png){width=960} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} predict_parts(explainer, new_observation = X_explain[1, ], type = "break_down") |> plot() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_evaluation_files/figure-html/shap-local-2.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ## What explanations do **not** mean 1. **Not causal.** SHAP and PDP describe the *fitted function*. "BMI drives risk up after 27.5" is a statement about the model, not about biology. 2. **Not unique.** Correlated predictors swap credit between fits; check stability across resamples before you tell a story. 3. **Not a safety certificate.** Use explanations to *audit*: agreement with what you know → trust up; disagreement → either you learned something or the model is cheating. Find out which. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} saveRDS(list(thr = thr_chosen, calibrator = calibrator), "outputs/t06_decisions.rds") ``` ::: ## Your turn (10 min) ::: {.callout-tip icon=false} ## Task A · Two use cases, two thresholds | Use case | Requirement | Why | |---|---|---| | Community screen | sensitivity ≥ 0.85 | a missed case costs years of silent disease; a false alarm costs one blood test | | Confirmatory pre-selection (limited lab budget) | specificity ≥ 0.90 | we can only afford to test a few; they had better be real | Find both thresholds on `cv_preds`; report flagged %, sensitivity, specificity, PPV and number-needed-to-screen on the **test** set. Then write the community-screen result as one sentence for a district health officer. **A2.** The model was validated at 11.6 % prevalence; the district's true prevalence is 6 %. Which numbers change, and which way? ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Solution A ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} thr <- threshold_perf(cv_preds, undx_dm, .pred_Yes, thresholds = seq(0.02, 0.80, by = 0.01)) thr_screen <- thr |> filter(.metric == "sensitivity", .estimate >= 0.85) |> slice_max(.threshold) |> pull(.threshold) thr_confirm <- thr |> filter(.metric == "specificity", .estimate >= 0.90) |> slice_min(.threshold) |> pull(.threshold) report_at <- function(preds, threshold) { preds |> mutate(.pred_rule = make_two_class_pred(.pred_Yes, levels = levels(undx_dm), threshold = threshold) |> as.factor()) |> summarise(threshold = threshold, flagged_pct = mean(.pred_rule == "Yes"), sens = sum(.pred_rule == "Yes" & undx_dm == "Yes") / sum(undx_dm == "Yes"), spec = sum(.pred_rule == "No" & undx_dm == "No") / sum(undx_dm == "No"), ppv = sum(.pred_rule == "Yes" & undx_dm == "Yes") / sum(.pred_rule == "Yes"), nns = 1 / ppv) } bind_rows(screen = report_at(test_preds, thr_screen), confirm = report_at(test_preds, thr_confirm), .id = "use_case") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ppv_at(0.85, 0.65, 0.116); ppv_at(0.85, 0.65, 0.06) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.2416667 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.1342105 ``` ::: ::: A model sentence: *"Testing the ~40 % of adults the model flags would find ~85 % of undiagnosed cases; about four people tested per case found."* A2: sensitivity and specificity are (roughly) properties of model + threshold and stay put; **PPV falls** (fewer true cases among the flagged), NPV rises, number-needed-to-screen rises; the flagged percentage also shifts because the score distribution changes with the population. ::: ::: {.callout-tip icon=false} ## Task B · Does it work equally well for everyone? Using `collect_predictions(xgb_last)` joined back to `dm_test`, compute AUC and sensitivity at `thr_chosen` by `sex` and by `ethnic`. Any group the model under-serves? What would you do about it? ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Solution B ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} by_group <- test_preds |> bind_cols(dm_test |> select(sex, ethnic)) |> # last_fit predictions are in test-set row order mutate(.pred_screen = make_two_class_pred(.pred_Yes, levels = levels(undx_dm), threshold = thr_chosen) |> as.factor()) by_group |> group_by(sex) |> roc_auc(undx_dm, .pred_Yes) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} by_group |> group_by(ethnic) |> roc_auc(undx_dm, .pred_Yes) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} by_group |> group_by(sex) |> sensitivity(undx_dm, .pred_screen) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Small groups (Others, Other Bumiputera) have wide uncertainty; look at the SE before reading a difference. If one group is genuinely under-flagged at the shared threshold, options are group-specific thresholds, re-weighting, more data — and, always, saying so in the paper. `fairmodels` extends DALEX with the standard fairness metrics. ::: ## What to remember 1. Accuracy lies at 12 % prevalence. Report sens/spec/PPV/NPV at the threshold you will use, at the prevalence you face. 2. ROC to compare models; PR and gain for what the predictions are worth; Brier and a calibration plot for honesty. 3. Choose the threshold from the use case, on CV predictions; report it on the test set, in people. 4. SMOTE moves the threshold in disguise and breaks calibration. Move the threshold instead. 5. Importance → *which*; PDP → *how*; SHAP → *why this person*. None of it is causal. **Next (14.00):** Tutorial 7 — neural networks.
